cse-1992-a-2-xi.approach: Deadlock is impossible when, even with every process holding one drive less than its maximum, at least one drive is still free: $n(k-1)+1 \le R$.

steps.title: Worst case allocation
steps.body: Each process needs $k = 3$ drives. The worst state is every process holding $k-1 = 2$ drives and waiting for one more. That uses $2n$ drives.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body:
If one more drive is free, some process finishes and releases its drives, so no deadlock:
$$2n + 1 \le 6 \;\Rightarrow\; n \le 2.5 \;\Rightarrow\; n_{\max} = 2$$

steps.title: Check $n = 3$
steps.body: With $n = 3$ each process can hold $2$ drives: $3 \times 2 = 6$ drives are used, none is free and all three wait forever, so deadlock is possible.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2 \times 2 + 1 = 5 \le 6$: always deadlock free, and it is the largest such $n$.
$3 \times 2 = 6$: all drives can be held with every process still waiting, so deadlock is possible.
Even worse than 3: $4$ processes can each hold one or two drives and block.
$n = 1$ is deadlock free but it is not the **maximum** value.

pitfalls: Dividing $6/3 = 2$ gives the right number here by coincidence; the correct test is $n(k-1)+1 \le R$.
cse-1992-a-2-xi.verification: For $n = 2$ the worst case uses $4$ drives and leaves $2$ free, so one process can always complete.

cse-1992-a-2-xii.approach: SPOOL = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line: output of many jobs is buffered on disk and fed to a slow, non-shareable device one job at a time. The classic example is a line printer.

steps.title: What spooling needs
steps.body: A slow device that can serve only one job at a time, while many jobs produce data for it. Jobs write to a disk spool area and a spooler process feeds the device sequentially.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: A line printer shared by many jobs fits exactly: each job’s output is spooled to disk and printed in turn. A terminal is interactive and the paging disk is used directly by the VM system, so neither is spooled.

answer.value: A line printer printing the output of several jobs

optionAnalysis.reason: An interactive terminal used for program input must respond in real time; it is not spooled.
The paging device in virtual memory is the backing store itself, accessed on demand, not a spooled device.
The textbook spooled device: output from many jobs is queued on disk and printed one job at a time.
Option C is correct, so “none of the above” is false.

cse-1992-a-2-xii.verification: Standard OS texts (Silberschatz, Tanenbaum) all use the printer as the spooling example.

cse-1992-a-2-xiii.approach: Test the three definitions on a tiny grammar, then argue generally: a rightmost derivation can always stop with $A$ as the rightmost non-terminal and terminals after it, but a leftmost derivation cannot expand anything to the right of an unexpanded $A$.

steps.title: A small grammar
steps.body: Take $S \to AB,\; A \to c,\; B \to b$. $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{b\}$ because $S \Rightarrow AB \Rightarrow Ab$ is a sentential form.

steps.title: Left-sentential forms
steps.body: Leftmost derivation: $S \Rightarrow AB \Rightarrow cB \Rightarrow cb$. The only form containing $A$ is $AB$, where $A$ is followed by the non-terminal $B$, so $\text{LFOLLOW}(A) = \varnothing \ne \text{FOLLOW}(A)$. Hence (a) is true and (c) is false.

steps.title: Right-sentential forms
steps.body:
Rightmost derivation: $S \Rightarrow AB \Rightarrow Ab \Rightarrow cb$, so $\text{RFOLLOW}(A) = \{b\}$.

In general, if $\alpha A a \beta$ is a sentential form, replace $\beta$ by a terminal string $y$ it derives; build the parse tree and expand its nodes right-to-left, stopping when $A$ is reached. Every expansion is of the rightmost non-terminal, and the form reached is $\gamma A a y$ — a right-sentential form. So every $a \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ is in $\text{RFOLLOW}(A)$ (and trivially conversely): (b) is true.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: $\text{RFOLLOW} = \text{FOLLOW}$ always, while $\text{LFOLLOW}$ may differ. True statements: (a) and (b).

optionAnalysis.reason: The grammar $S \to AB$ gives $\text{LFOLLOW}(A) = \varnothing$ but $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{b\}$.
A rightmost derivation can expand everything right of $A$ to terminals first, so every follower of $A$ appears in some right-sentential form.
Contradicted by the same example: LFOLLOW differs.
FOLLOW and RFOLLOW are always equal, so the three can never all be different.

pitfalls: Assuming leftmost and rightmost derivations reach the same sentential forms — they reach the same **sentences**, not the same intermediate forms.
cse-1992-a-2-xiii.verification: Checked the example by listing every leftmost and rightmost form of $S \to AB,\, A \to c,\, B \to b$.

cse-1992-a-2-xiv.approach: SLR(1) and LALR(1) are built on the same LR(0) item-set cores (LALR merges LR(1) states with equal cores), so the state machine — shifts and gotos — is identical. Only the look-aheads used for reductions differ: FOLLOW sets for SLR, propagated look-aheads for LALR.

steps.title: Same states
steps.body: LALR(1) states = LR(1) states merged by core = the LR(0) collection used by SLR(1). Same states and same transitions, so **shift** entries and the **goto** part are identical.

steps.title: Different reduce look-aheads
steps.body: SLR puts reduce $A \to \alpha$ on every terminal in $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$; LALR only on its look-ahead set, which is a subset of $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$. So some reduce entries in SLR are blank (error) in LALR: **reduce** and **error** entries may differ.

optionAnalysis.reason: Goto entries come from the transitions of the LR(0) automaton, which both tables share.
Shift entries are also transitions of the same automaton, hence identical.
LALR look-aheads $\subseteq$ FOLLOW, so SLR may have extra reduce entries.
Where SLR reduces and LALR does not, LALR has an error entry — error entries differ.

pitfalls: Thinking LALR has more states than SLR — that is canonical LR(1), not LALR.
cse-1992-a-2-xiv.verification: Classic grammar $S \to L{=}R \mid R,\; L \to {*}R \mid id,\; R \to L$: SLR reduces $R \to L$ on ‘=’ (conflict), LALR does not — the reduce/error entries differ while shifts match.

cse-1992-a-2-xv.approach: Check each implication: try to prove it in general, otherwise build a two-element counter-model.

steps.title: (a) is valid
steps.body: If $\forall x\,P(x)$ holds, then every $x$ satisfies $P(x) \lor Q(x)$; likewise if $\forall x\,Q(x)$ holds. Either way $\forall x\,\{P(x) \lor Q(x)\}$.

steps.title: Counter-models for (b), (c)
steps.body:
Domain $\{1, 2\}$, $P = \{1\}$, $Q = \{2\}$.

- (b): $\exists P$ and $\exists Q$ are true, but no element has both, so $\exists(P \land Q)$ is false.
- (c): every element is in $P$ or $Q$, so $\forall(P \lor Q)$ is true, but neither $\forall P$ nor $\forall Q$ holds.

steps.title: Counter-model for (d)
steps.body: $P$ true everywhere, $Q$ false everywhere: $\exists x\{P \lor Q\}$ is true, $\sim\forall x P(x)$ is false and $\exists x Q(x)$ is false, so the implication fails.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\forall$ distributes over $\lor$ in this direction.
$\exists$ does not distribute over $\land$: $P = \{1\},\, Q = \{2\}$.
Converse of (a) fails with the same model.
$P \equiv$ true, $Q \equiv$ false makes the antecedent true and the consequent false.

cse-1992-a-2-xv.verification: Each invalid option has an explicit finite counter-model; (a) has a direct proof.

cse-1992-a-2-xvi.approach: An implication is a tautology iff it can never have a true antecedent and a false consequent; try to falsify each one.

steps.title: (b) cannot be falsified
steps.body: To falsify $a \land b \to b \lor c$ we need $a \land b = 1$, so $b = 1$; but then $b \lor c = 1$. Impossible — tautology.

steps.title: Falsify the others
steps.body:
- (a) $a = 1, b = 0$: $a \lor b = 1$, $b \land c = 0$ → false.
- (c) $a = b = 1, c = 0$: $1 \to (1 \to 0) = 1 \to 0 = 0$.
- (d) $a = b = 1, c = 0$: either grouping gives $0$ — right-associated $1 \to (1 \to 0) = 0$; left-associated $(1 \to 1) \to (1 \to 0) = 1 \to 0 = 0$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $a = 1, b = 0$ falsifies it.
True antecedent forces $b = 1$, which makes the consequent true.
$a = b = 1, c = 0$ falsifies it.
$a = b = 1, c = 0$ falsifies it under either bracketing.

cse-1992-a-2-xvi.verification: Each non-tautology has a falsifying assignment; (b) was checked by contradiction.

cse-1992-a-2-xvii.approach: Read (a) and (b) as the standard identities $(r^*)^* = r^*$ and $(r^*s^*)^* = (r+s)^*$ (the scan lost the outer star), then test each with small strings.

steps.title: (a) and (b) are true
steps.body:
- $(r^*)^* = r^*$: concatenating strings of $r^*$ gives a string of $r^*$.
- $(r^*s^*)^* = (r+s)^*$: $r^*s^* \supseteq \{r, s\}$, so its star contains every string over $r, s$; conversely every piece is in $(r+s)^*$.

steps.title: (c) and (d) are false
steps.body: Take $r = a$, $s = b$. The string $ab$ is in $(a+b)^*$ and in $a^*b^*$ but not in $a^* + b^*$, so (c) and (d) both fail. Also $ba \in (a+b)^*$ but $ba \notin a^*b^*$, which is why (b) needs the outer star.

optionAnalysis.reason: $(r^*)^* = r^*$ — idempotence of star.
With the outer star, $(r^*s^*)^* = (r+s)^*$. Without it (as scanned), $ba$ would be a counterexample.
$ab \in (a+b)^*$ but $ab \notin a^* + b^*$.
$ab \in a^*b^*$ but $ab \notin a^* + b^*$.

cse-1992-a-2-xvii.verification: Checked each identity with r = a, s = b on strings of length ≤ 2.

cse-1992-a-2-xviii.approach: In CNF every rule is $A \to BC$ (adds one symbol) or $A \to a$ (turns a variable into a terminal). Count how many of each are needed for a string of length $l$.

steps.title: Grow to $l$ variables
steps.body: Start with $1$ symbol ($S$). Each $A \to BC$ step increases the length by $1$, so reaching $l$ symbols takes $l - 1$ steps.

steps.title: Turn them into terminals
steps.body:
Each of the $l$ variables needs one $A \to a$ step: $l$ steps.
$$(l - 1) + l = 2l - 1$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $2l$ over-counts by one: only $l - 1$ binary steps are needed.
$2l + 1$ over-counts by two.
$(l - 1)$ binary rules $+$ $l$ terminal rules.
$l$ counts only the terminal rules.

cse-1992-a-2-xviii.verification: $l = 1$: $S \to a$ is $1 = 2(1) - 1$ step. $l = 2$: $S \to AB \to aB \to ab$ is $3 = 2(2) - 1$ steps.

cse-1992-a-2-xix.approach: Recall the closure table for CFLs: union, concatenation and star are closed (grammar constructions); intersection and complement are not.

steps.title: Closed operations
steps.body:
- Union: $S \to S_1 \mid S_2$.
- Kleene star: $S \to S S_1 \mid \varepsilon$.

steps.title: Not closed
steps.body: Intersection: $\{a^nb^nc^m\} \cap \{a^mb^nc^n\} = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$, which is not context-free. Complement: $L_1 \cap L_2 = \overline{\overline{L_1} \cup \overline{L_2}}$, so closure under complement plus union would give closure under intersection — contradiction.

answer.value: Closed under union and Kleene closure

optionAnalysis.reason: $S \to S_1 \mid S_2$.
Not closed: would imply closure under intersection via De Morgan.
$\{a^nb^nc^m\} \cap \{a^mb^nc^n\} = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not a CFL.
$S \to S S_1 \mid \varepsilon$.

cse-1992-a-2-xix.verification: $a^nb^nc^n$ fails the pumping lemma for CFLs, confirming the intersection counterexample.

cse-1992-a-2-xx.approach: Recall which machine classes lose power when made deterministic: finite automata and Turing machines do not; pushdown automata do.

steps.title: NFA and NTM
steps.body: NFA → DFA by the subset construction (at most $2^n$ states). An NTM is simulated by a DTM that explores its computation tree breadth-first, accepting the same language.

steps.title: NPDA
steps.body: $\{ww^R\}$ is accepted by an NPDA (guess the middle) but by no DPDA, since a DPDA cannot know where the middle is. Deterministic CFLs are a proper subset of CFLs.

optionAnalysis.reason: Subset construction gives an equivalent DFA.
$ww^R$ is an NPDA language with no equivalent DPDA.
Breadth-first simulation of the computation tree gives an equivalent DTM.
The statement holds for (a) and (c).

cse-1992-a-2-xx.verification: Matches the standard hierarchy: DFA = NFA, DPDA ⊊ NPDA, DTM = NTM.

cse-1992-a-3-i.approach: Trace each macro for the value of X that triggers its recursive call (X = 0) and see whether the argument of the recursive call changes.

steps.title: Trace M1 0
steps.body: $X = 0$: \`.IF EQ\` is true → expands \`M1 1\`. Now $X = 1$: \`.IF EQ\` false, \`.IF NE\` true → emits \`.WORD 1\` and stops. M1 always terminates (at most one recursive level).

steps.title: Trace M2 0
steps.body: $X = 0$: \`.IF EQ\` true → expands \`M2 X\` with the **same** $X = 0$, which again takes the same branch → \`M2 0\` → … forever. Any call with a non-zero argument just emits \`.WORD X+1\`.

answer.value: M2 — e.g. the call `M2 0` recurses forever

pitfalls: M1 also calls itself when X = 0, but with X+1, so the recursion ends after one level.
cse-1992-a-3-i.verification: Only an argument equal to zero triggers recursion; M1 changes it, M2 does not.

cse-1992-a-3-ii.approach: Pass 1 defines symbols (location counter, symbol and literal tables); pass 2 uses those tables to generate code and the listing.

steps.title: Pass 1 work
steps.body: Scans the source, advances the location counter, enters labels in the symbol table and literals in the literal table, assigning them addresses. So (b) literals → pass 1, and (d) the addresses of local symbols are determined in pass 1.

steps.title: Pass 2 work
steps.body: Re-reads the source, looks every symbol up, assembles the object code and prints the listing (which shows the object code). So (a) → pass 2 and (c) → pass 2.

pitfalls: (d) is sometimes read as “substituting addresses into instructions”, which happens in pass 2; the address values themselves are fixed in pass 1.
cse-1992-a-3-ii.verification: Consistent with the classic two-pass design (Beck, Dhamdhere).

cse-1992-a-3-iii.approach: Each component is a tree; a tree on $n_i$ vertices has $n_i - 1$ edges. Sum over the $p$ components.

steps.title: Per component
steps.body: Component $i$ is a tree with $n_i$ vertices, so it has $n_i - 1$ edges, where $n_1 + \dots + n_p = n$.

cse-1992-a-3-iii.verification: $p = 1$ gives a tree with $n - 1$ edges; $p = n$ (isolated vertices) gives $0$ edges.

cse-1992-a-3-iv.approach: Quicksort is worst when every partition is maximally unbalanced (sizes $k-1$ and $0$). With the last element as pivot this happens when the pivot is always the largest (or smallest) remaining element — i.e. sorted or reverse-sorted input.

steps.title: Sorted input
steps.body: Input $1, 2, \dots, n$. Pivot $= n$ (largest): all others go left, right part empty. Recursion on $1, \dots, n-1$ again picks the largest, and so on.

scene.label: A
scene.caption: Pass 1: pivot 5 — left part {1..4}, right part empty

steps.title: Next passes
steps.body: Each pass removes only the pivot.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: Comparisons $= (n-1) + (n-2) + \dots + 1 = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)$, the maximum. Reverse order $n, \dots, 1$ also gives pivot $=$ smallest every time and the same cost.

answer.value: Already sorted input $1, 2, \dots, n$ (reverse order $n, \dots, 1$ works too)

pitfalls: Random-looking input usually gives balanced splits; the worst case comes from (reverse) sorted data with a fixed-position pivot.

cse-1992-a-3-v.approach: This is Belady’s anomaly, which only non-stack algorithms show; FIFO is the classic example.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Reference string $1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5$ under FIFO: $9$ faults with $3$ frames but $10$ faults with $4$ frames.

steps.title: Why not LRU / OPT
steps.body: LRU and optimal are stack algorithms: the pages held with k frames are always a subset of those held with k+1 frames, so faults can never increase.

cse-1992-a-3-v.verification: The 12-reference string above is Belady’s original counterexample.

cse-1992-b-4-a.approach: Overflow happens when the true sum does not fit the signed range, which shows up as the carry into the sign bit differing from the carry out of it.

steps.title: Carry out is not overflow
steps.body: 4-bit: $-1 + 1 = 1111 + 0001 = 1\,0000$. There is a carry out, but the result $0000 = 0$ is correct — no overflow.

steps.title: Overflow without carry out
steps.body: $7 + 1 = 0111 + 0001 = 1000 = -8$: wrong sign. Carry **into** the MSB is $1$, carry **out** is $0$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: $$V = C_{n-1} \oplus C_n$$ where $C_{n-1}$ is the carry into the MSB and $C_n$ the carry out. Equivalently: both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign. Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow.

answer.value: Overflow iff carry into MSB $\ne$ carry out of MSB ($V = C_{n-1} \oplus C_n$), i.e. same-sign operands give a result of the other sign

cse-1992-b-4-b.approach: Assign codes A → 11, B → 10, C → 01, none → 00, write $X_1, X_0$ as functions of A, B, C, then use A, B as the select lines of two 4:1 MUXes with data inputs from {0, 1, C}.

steps.title: Output functions
steps.body:
$X_1 = 1$ when A or B is active: $X_1 = A + B$.
$X_0 = 1$ for A, or for C with A, B inactive: $X_0 = A + \overline{A}\,\overline{B}\,C = A + \overline{B}C$.

steps.title: MUX data inputs
steps.body:
Select lines $S_1S_0 = AB$; each data input is the function with A, B fixed:

| $AB$ | $X_1$ MUX input | $X_0$ MUX input |
|---|---|---|
| 00 | 0 | $C$ |
| 01 | 1 | 0 |
| 10 | 1 | 1 |
| 11 | 1 | 1 |

steps.title: Circuit
steps.body: Two 4:1 MUXes share selects $S_1 = A$, $S_0 = B$. MUX 1 inputs $(I_0..I_3) = (0, 1, 1, 1)$ gives $X_1$; MUX 2 inputs $(C, 0, 1, 1)$ gives $X_0$. No other gates are needed.

answer.value: $X_1 = A + B$, $X_0 = A + \overline{B}C$; with $S_1S_0 = AB$: $X_1$ MUX inputs $0,1,1,1$ and $X_0$ MUX inputs $C,0,1,1$ (codes A = 11, B = 10, C = 01)

pitfalls: The paper does not fix the output codes; any one-to-one assignment with none → 00 works, but the MUX inputs change accordingly.

cse-1992-b-4-c.approach: A counter where only one flip-flop changes per clock is a Gray-code counter. For D flip-flops $D_i = Q_i^{+}$, so read each next-state bit off the state table and minimise with a K-map.

steps.title: State table
steps.body: 3-bit Gray sequence $000 \to 001 \to 011 \to 010 \to 110 \to 111 \to 101 \to 100 \to 000$. Since $D = Q^{+}$, the D columns equal the next state.

steps.title: Circuit
steps.body: Three D flip-flops on a common clock with the inputs above (two AND-OR networks and one XNOR). Each transition flips exactly one bit, including the wrap-around $100 \to 000$.

answer.value: Gray-code counter $000\to001\to011\to010\to110\to111\to101\to100\to000$ with $D_2 = Q_1\overline{Q_0} + Q_2Q_0$, $D_1 = \overline{Q_2}Q_0 + Q_1\overline{Q_0}$, $D_0 = \overline{Q_2 \oplus Q_1}$

pitfalls: A binary counter fails: 011 → 100 changes all three bits.

cse-1992-b-5-a.approach: Weight reads and writes separately: a read hits the cache (50 ns) with probability 0.9 and otherwise goes to main memory (500 ns); with write-through every write costs a main-memory access (500 ns).
cse-1992-b-5-a.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $t_m$ | 500 ns |
| $t_c$ | 50 ns |
| reads / writes | 80% / 20% |
| read hit ratio | 0.9 |

steps.title: Write time
steps.body: Write-through updates cache and memory simultaneously, so a write takes the memory time: $t_w = 500$ ns.

pitfalls: If a read miss is charged as cache look-up + memory ($550$ ns), $t_r = 45 + 55 = 100$ and $t_{avg} = 80 + 100 = 180$ ns — state the assumption.
cse-1992-b-5-a.verification: Bounds: all-cache would be 50 ns, all-memory 500 ns; $176$ lies between and is pulled up by the 20% writes ($100$ ns of it).

cse-1992-b-5-b.approach: Connect the highest-priority device to the highest-priority line (A→INTR1, B→INTR2, C→INTR3). Gate each request with a bit of the interrupt mask register, then let a priority network pass only the highest unmasked request and raise INT to the CPU.

steps.title: Line assignment
steps.body: Priority of A > B > C must follow the line priorities, so A drives INTR1, B drives INTR2 and C drives INTR3.

steps.title: Masking
steps.body: Mask register bits $M_1, M_2, M_3$ (set by software). Effective requests: $I_1 = R_A M_1$, $I_2 = R_B M_2$, $I_3 = R_C M_3$. A masked device cannot interrupt even if it requests.

steps.title: Priority logic
steps.body:
$$G_A = I_1,\quad G_B = \overline{I_1}\,I_2,\quad G_C = \overline{I_1}\,\overline{I_2}\,I_3$$
$$\text{INT} = \text{IEN}\cdot(I_1 + I_2 + I_3)$$
The grants (or a priority encoder with outputs $x y$) form the vector address placed on the bus when the CPU acknowledges.

scene.caption: B and C request, A idle: only GB = 1 and INT = 1

steps.title: Example
steps.body: B and C request with all masks set: $I_1 = 0$, $I_2 = I_3 = 1$, so $G_B = 1$, $G_C = 0$ and INT $= 1$ — B is serviced. Clearing $M_2$ would make $G_C = 1$ instead.

answer.value: Parallel priority logic: A, B, C drive INTR1, INTR2, INTR3; each request is ANDed with its mask-register bit ($I_k = R_k M_k$), then priority gating gives $G_A = I_1$, $G_B = \overline{I_1}I_2$, $G_C = \overline{I_1}\,\overline{I_2}I_3$, and INT to the CPU $= \text{IEN}\cdot(I_1 + I_2 + I_3)$; the grant/encoder output selects the vector of the highest-priority unmasked device

pitfalls: A daisy chain uses one shared request line and no mask register — not what the question describes.
cse-1992-b-5-b.verification: Checked all three single-request cases: each sets only its own grant; with two requests the higher-priority grant wins.
